prohibited_recommendations: Do NOT delay empiric antimicrobial therapy while awaiting imaging or LP results when bacterial meningitis is clinically suspected.
Do not perform lumbar puncture before cranial imaging in this patient: asplenia (a severe immunocompromised state) is an imaging-first criterion under WHO 2025 section A.4.
Do NOT rely on a negative Gram stain or a 'normal CT' to rule out bacterial meningitis when the clinical syndrome is present.
Do NOT treat with oral antibiotics alone; CNS penetration is inadequate for meningitis.
required_recommendations: Give ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 12 hours (or cefotaxime 2 g IV every 6 hours) within 60 minutes of clinical suspicion, after blood cultures and without waiting for imaging or lumbar puncture (WHO 2025, strong recommendation). Add vancomycin only where pneumococcal resistance to penicillin or third-generation cephalosporins is highly prevalent locally (WHO 2025, conditional recommendation).
Add ampicillin 2 g IV every 4 hours for Listeria monocytogenes cover because of diabetes mellitus and asplenia (WHO 2025, strong recommendation).

Give dexamethasone 10 mg IV every 6 hours, starting shortly before or with the first antibiotic dose; continue for a maximum of 4 days if S. pneumoniae or H. influenzae type b is identified, and stop it once another organism is identified (WHO 2025). Continue for 4 days: Haemophilus influenzae type b is identified.
Draw two sets of peripheral blood cultures before the first antibiotic dose.

Take blood cultures and give the first dose of empirical antibiotics with dexamethasone before cranial imaging; obtain a CT head before lumbar puncture because of asplenia (a severe immunocompromised state) (WHO 2025 section A.4); neither imaging nor lumbar puncture may delay treatment.
Send full CSF panel (cell count, differential, glucose, protein, Gram stain, culture, meningitis multiplex PCR, lactate) at the LP.

Treat sepsis with hypoperfusion (blood pressure 92/58 mmHg, lactate 3.8 mmol/L): IV crystalloid resuscitation, vasopressors if the mean arterial pressure stays below 65 mmHg, repeat lactate, and serial platelets, INR, fibrinogen and D-dimer for evolving DIC.

Narrow therapy once the organism and susceptibilities are known: Haemophilus influenzae type b, beta-lactamase positive and ampicillin resistant, susceptible to ceftriaxone, so stop ampicillin and any vancomycin and continue ceftriaxone.
Place patient on droplet precautions until meningococcal disease is excluded and for the first 24 hours of effective therapy.

Recognise asplenia and ensure coverage of encapsulated organisms (S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis, H. influenzae); arrange post-recovery Hib, meningococcal and pneumococcal conjugate vaccination per ACIP.
Arrange formal audiological assessment before discharge, or within 4 weeks of discharge if it cannot be done before (WHO 2025, strong recommendation).
Resuscitate the hypotension before the lumbar puncture (WHO 2025 A.1.1); antibiotics and dexamethasone are not delayed for it.

avoided_actions.rationale: No murmur or other sign of endocarditis; Haemophilus influenzae bacteremia with meningitis does not call for echocardiography in the meningitis work-up.
No arrhythmia indication; continuous cardiac monitoring contributes nothing to meningitis diagnosis or treatment.
PET imaging has no role in acute meningitis diagnosis; CT and MRI cover the indications.
Amyloid PET is a dementia biomarker tool with no role in acute infectious meningitis.

accepted: Acute bacterial meningitis due to Haemophilus influenzae type b in an asplenic adult

differential.key_features: Raised by the preceding upper respiratory illness and the negative Gram stain; excluded: neutrophilic CSF (380 cells, 72% neutrophils) with glucose ratio 0.16, protein 168 mg/dL and lactate 6.2 mmol/L, Haemophilus influenzae on PCR and in both blood culture sets, no viral panel target detected.
Raised by asplenia without meningococcal vaccination, hypotension and coagulopathy; no rash; Neisseria meningitidis not detected on PCR and Haemophilus influenzae type b grown from blood.
Diabetes and asplenia make empirical ampicillin necessary; Listeria not detected on PCR and the isolate is Haemophilus influenzae type b.
No seizure or focal temporal features; neutrophilic rather than lymphocytic CSF; HSV-1 and HSV-2 not detected on PCR.
The earlier emergency department diagnosis; vomiting and loose stools fit, but nuchal rigidity, photophobia and a bacterial CSF establish meningitis.
Subacute onset, lymphocytic CSF, basilar enhancement; the 24-hour course after a week-long respiratory illness and the neutrophilic CSF with a named organism do not fit.

key_clinical_evidence: Acute bacterial meningitis presents with fever, headache, meningismus, and altered mental status; the full triad is present in only ~40%, so partial syndromes warrant aggressive workup.
Antibiotics are given within 60 minutes of suspicion; neither imaging nor lumbar puncture may delay them (WHO 2025).

Take blood cultures and give the first dose of empirical antibiotics with dexamethasone before cranial imaging; obtain a CT head before lumbar puncture because of asplenia (a severe immunocompromised state) (WHO 2025 section A.4); neither imaging nor lumbar puncture may delay treatment.

Give dexamethasone 10 mg IV every 6 hours, starting shortly before or with the first antibiotic dose; continue for a maximum of 4 days if S. pneumoniae or H. influenzae type b is identified, and stop it once another organism is identified (WHO 2025).

A negative Gram stain does not exclude bacterial meningitis: sensitivity is about 85% with wide confidence limits (WHO 2025), lower after antibiotics; culture and multiplex PCR establish the organism.
A CSF:blood glucose ratio of 0.4 or less is abnormally low (WHO 2025 A.2.2) and is more informative than the absolute value, above all in hyperglycemia.

Empirical therapy is ceftriaxone or cefotaxime within 60 minutes, with ampicillin when a Listeria risk factor (age over 60, pregnancy, immunocompromise) is present; vancomycin only where pneumococcal resistance is locally prevalent (WHO 2025).

Asplenia (anatomic or functional) dramatically increases risk of overwhelming infection with encapsulated organisms (S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis, H. influenzae); these patients require lifelong vaccination and a low threshold for empiric antibiotics.
A beta-lactamase-producing Haemophilus influenzae is resistant to amoxicillin, which explains progression on oral amoxicillin; third-generation cephalosporins remain active.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Prior antibiotics reduce Gram-stain and culture yield; with neutrophilic pleocytosis, a CSF:blood glucose ratio of 0.16 and raised CSF lactate the diagnosis remains bacterial meningitis, and the multiplex PCR and blood cultures identify Haemophilus influenzae.
red_herrings.data_point: Negative CSF Gram stain in a patient with prior oral antibiotic exposure
red_herrings.intended_effect: Suggest viral or aseptic meningitis and lower the threshold for withholding empiric antibiotics.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Parameningeal sinus disease can be a SOURCE of bacterial meningitis (here S. pneumoniae or H. influenzae type b are the expected organisms), not an alternative diagnosis; the CSF profile remains the deciding evidence.
red_herrings.data_point: Incidental right maxillary sinus mucosal thickening on CT
red_herrings.intended_effect: Suggest uncomplicated sinusitis as the source of headache and fever, deferring meningitis evaluation.

sequence_constraints.reason: Under WHO 2025 section A.4 cranial imaging is not performed routinely; where readily accessible it precedes lumbar puncture when any of these is present at presentation: Glasgow Coma Score below 10, focal neurological signs, cranial nerve deficits, papilledema, new-onset seizures in adults, or a severe immunocompromised state. Here: asplenia (severe immunocompromised state). NICE NG240 does not cover this patient (asplenia is an immunodeficiency outside its scope). Blood cultures and the first antibiotic dose with dexamethasone come before imaging, which must not delay them.
Blood cultures are taken, and empirical antibiotics with dexamethasone given, before cranial imaging; imaging must not delay treatment (WHO 2025).

metadata.condition_name: Acute bacterial meningitis (Haemophilus influenzae type b)
metadata.difficulty_description: Moderate difficulty: asplenic patient with bacterial meningitis partially treated with oral amoxicillin. Key confounders include a negative Gram stain after prior oral antibiotics, an initial misdiagnosis as viral gastroenteritis, leukopenia rather than leukocytosis, an incidental mildly elevated TSH, and maxillary sinusitis as a potential distraction. The multiplex PCR and blood cultures identify a beta-lactamase-producing Haemophilus influenzae type b.
metadata.difficulty_rationale: 4 required actions; 2 red herrings; asplenia broadens encapsulated-organism risk
metadata.revision_reason: Reviewer 2 meningitis audit: complete LP/microbiology/lab pathway, no ECG, and MRI restricted to complications or non-response

patient.history_present_illness: A 52-year-old man with a history of splenectomy, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and hypertension presents to the emergency department with progressive drowsiness and confusion over the past 24 hours. His illness began approximately one week ago with rhinorrhea, nonproductive cough, mild sore throat, and low-grade fevers, for which he was evaluated at an urgent care center three days prior to presentation and started on oral amoxicillin for a presumed upper respiratory tract infection. He initially felt mildly improved, but yesterday he developed worsening fever, nausea, and three episodes of nonbloody, nonbilious vomiting. His wife reports he also had two episodes of loose stools and was unable to keep down fluids. She took him to a nearby emergency department where he was diagnosed with viral gastroenteritis, treated with intravenous ondansetron and a one-liter normal saline bolus, and discharged home with instructions for supportive care. Over the ensuing 12 hours, his condition deteriorated substantially. His wife noticed he became increasingly lethargic, was difficult to arouse, and seemed confused when he did speak, calling her by the wrong name and making nonsensical statements. He complained of a severe diffuse headache before becoming too drowsy to communicate effectively. She denies any observed seizure activity, limb shaking, tongue biting, or urinary incontinence. She has not noted any rash, skin changes, or recent insect bites. There is no history of recent travel outside the region, no known sick contacts with meningitis, and no exposure to crowded living conditions. His vaccination history is notable for incomplete post-splenectomy immunization — he received a pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine but never received the Haemophilus influenzae type b conjugate vaccine or a meningococcal vaccine. Paramedics report that during transport his temperature was 39.2 degrees Celsius and he had fluctuating levels of consciousness.

neurological_exam.additional: Mild nuchal rigidity detected on passive flexion of the neck, though the patient does not have classic Kernig or Brudzinski signs. Mild photosensitivity noted — patient turns away from penlight. No rash or petechiae. Tonsils mildly enlarged and erythematous. Diffuse mild abdominal tenderness without guarding or rebound.
neurological_exam.coordination: Unable to assess due to altered mental status.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils 3 mm bilaterally with sluggish but present reaction to light. No papilledema on fundoscopy. Corneal reflexes intact. No facial asymmetry noted. Gag reflex present. Unable to assess visual fields or extraocular movements reliably due to poor cooperation.
neurological_exam.gait: Unable to assess; patient is bedbound.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Glasgow Coma Scale 11 (E3 V3 M5). Patient is drowsy but arousable to voice and painful stimuli. Opens eyes to voice. Verbal responses are inappropriate words only. Localizes pain. Oriented to person only, not to place or time. Unable to cooperate with formal cognitive testing due to altered level of consciousness.
neurological_exam.motor: Moves all extremities spontaneously but less on the right side than the left. Withdraws from painful stimuli in all limbs. No overt focal weakness appreciated, though subtle right-sided preference for guarding cannot be excluded. Muscle tone mildly increased diffusely.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Deep tendon reflexes 2+ and symmetric in biceps, triceps, brachioradialis, patellar, and Achilles bilaterally. Plantar responses equivocal bilaterally.
neurological_exam.sensory: Withdraws to pain symmetrically in all four extremities. Detailed sensory examination not possible due to encephalopathy.
